identity.variant: finite open chain; bit-flip and phase-flip basis conventions

card.description: A one-dimensional CSS stabilizer family whose adjacent-pair checks constrain an open chain to a two-dimensional, cat-like code space. In the bit-flip convention, Z_i Z_{i+1} checks turn X errors into domain-wall endpoints; global Hadamard conjugation exchanges X and Z to give the phase-flip convention. The protected logical string spans the chain, but its conjugate has a one-qubit representative, so the ordinary Pauli distance is one: this is a controlled memory for one biased Pauli sector, not protection against arbitrary Pauli noise.

views.description: The open-chain incidence matrix has one row for each neighboring pair. Reading it as Z checks diagnoses bit flips; reading it as X checks diagnoses phase flips. The constructor uses the same binary matrix in both cases, so the basis label changes the protected sector without changing the chain geometry.

In the bit-flip convention, X on every site commutes with all parities and is not a stabilizer, while Z on any one site is its conjugate logical. Their roles exchange in the phase-flip convention. This normalizer calculation exposes both the growing protected-sector distance and the weight-one logical that fixes the full quantum distance.

A connected string of protected-sector flips changes only the parities at its endpoints. Interior flips cancel from the syndrome because every interior check sees two changed qubits. Decoding therefore reconstructs a chain with the observed boundary, not the unknowable microscopic error itself.

Repeating the parity measurements adds a time direction. Differences between neighboring syndrome rounds become detection events, and a data fault and a measurement fault occupy differently oriented edges of a planar spacetime graph. Majority vote on the final data is therefore not a decoder for the circuit-level history.

Under a specified stochastic noise model, candidate error histories can be written as spin configurations and logical decoding compares their partition functions. This statistical-mechanical dictionary belongs to the decoder and noise model; it is not a second stabilizer family.

params.L: Number of data qubits in the finite open chain; integer L >= 2.
params.basis: Protected-sector convention: 'bit-flip' uses neighboring ZZ checks and 'phase-flip' uses neighboring XX checks.

decoders.noise: finite one-shot chain with independent protected-sector data flips, perfect final data readout, and no measurement faults
decoders.notes: Maximum likelihood reduces to majority inference for the symmetric independent model. Calling the rule “majority vote” is not enough to extend it to repeated noisy syndrome extraction: that setting has a different observation object and fault equivalence.

decoders.noise: repeated projective parity rounds with stochastic data and measurement faults represented by a calibrated planar spacetime detection graph
decoders.notes: Matching pairs detection events using edge weights derived from the admitted circuit model. Leakage, long-range correlations, and ambiguous multi-fault mechanisms require graph augmentation or a different decoder; no threshold is transferred to an unspecified circuit here.

decoders.noise: planar circuit-level repetition model whose logical sectors admit exact partition-function evaluation
decoders.notes: Exact maximum-likelihood decoding retains circuit correlations that an independently weighted matching graph can discard. Its exactness is scoped to the planar model and boundary conditions in the cited work, not to arbitrary leakage or correlated hardware noise.

realizations.description: Repeated stabilizer measurements were decoded from complete syndrome histories, and later increasing-chain experiments separately tested bit-flip and phase-flip suppression. These are one-sector, protocol- and decoder-specific results rather than arbitrary-state quantum memories.
Repeated correction cycles were implemented on a small ion register. The demonstration establishes closed protocol repetition at fixed size; it does not by itself supply a growing-family threshold.
Small spin-qubit blocks demonstrated bit-flip correction and a phase-flip-code implementation. Their control, readout, and noise-bias assumptions remain part of the realization claim.

A surface-code patch was split into two distance-three repetition blocks and used for a joint logical operation. This demonstrates the merge/split protocol and its decoding stack, not an operation native to an isolated chain with no ancillary geometry.

relations.how: Code deformation can split a suitable surface-code patch into two repetition blocks and later use their shared layout for joint parity processing. The finite boundary geometry, syndrome rounds, and decoder are part of the switch; an isolated chain is not identical to a surface code.

operations.cost: one parallel physical-Pauli layer on all L data qubits; X in the bit-flip convention and Z in the phase-flip convention

operations.gate: CNOT between aligned blocks in the same basis convention
operations.cost: one pairwise physical-CNOT layer between corresponding sites; routing, syndrome extraction, and correlated recovery remain additional

origin.method: binary conjugation of both blocks' parity checks and logical pair

operations.cost: one physical-H layer on every data qubit, exchanging neighboring ZZ and XX checks together with the protected and unprotected Pauli sectors

origin.method: H X H = Z and H Z H = X on every constructor stabilizer

operations.gate: joint logical parity between split repetition blocks
operations.cost: a surface-code-derived coupling region, merge/split syndrome rounds, ancilla measurements, correlated decoding, and feed-forward
